newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Energy crisis deepens in Russian Far East.
newsitem.headline: Energy crisis deepens in Russian Far East.

text.p: Miners in Russia's Far East vowed on Monday to step up their protests against unpaid wages and officials in the strategic port of Vladivostok predicted worsening power shortages.

In a press statement, the miners' union of the Pacific Primorsky Krai region said it was halting all coal deliveries to power stations because the authorities had failed to tackle wage arrears stretching back six months.
It said miners would hold a protest meeting in Vladivostok on Friday and called on the regional authorities to stop what it called "the destruction of the Far East mining industry".

The miners' plight is a familiar one in post-communist Russia. Millions of workers in private and public sectors go many months without pay due to a complex web of debt linking suppliers and customers, companies and government.

The regional power utility, Dalenergo, the main target of the miners' anger, said it had no money to pay them. It said customers, including the city administration. owed it more than two trillion roubles (around $400 milion).
Dalenergo reported a 1996 pre-tax loss of 39.57 billion roubles ($6.8 million) on sales of 2.71 trillion roubles ($470 million), according to figures released on Monday.
Vladivostok authorities last Thursday declared a state of emergency in the port city, allowing civil defence officials to take control of facilities requiring round-the-clock power.
"The Primorsky power station is currently receiving around 2,500 tonnes of coal a day, but it needs close to 20,000 tonnes to meet customers' needs," Dalenergo's Alexander Gelbakh said.
He said Vladivostok's half-million residents were receiving less than ten hours of electricity a day.
Regional governor Yevgeny Nazdratenko convened a gathering of mayors from the region to discuss the crisis, but the mayor of Vladivostok, Viktor Cherepkov, did not attend the meeting.
Cherepkov and Nazdratenko are political enemies. The mayor accuses the governor of helping engineer the energy crisis by refusing to permit higher electricity tariffs.
Cherpkov has also criticised Dalenergo for refusing to accept coal and fuel oil supplies from outside sources.

The mayor's office, describing the energy situation as catastrophic, accused Dalenergo in a statement of thwarting joint efforts by the miners and the city administration to ensure regular energy supplies to Vladivostok.
Behind the accusations and counter-accusations lies a simple economic reality, rooted in Russia's communist past of blanket state subsidies.

"The fact is that energy prices are too low. That is why Dalenergo has no money. Our consumers are convinced that they should receive electricity for free," Miners' Union leader Pyotr Kiryasov told Reuters.
"This is what we were all taught to expect under socialism."

Faced with the impasse, the politicians are turning to Moscow. Russian Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov is expected to visit Vladivostok on Tuesday, ostensibly to dicuss ways of improving tax collection, but local sources said the worsening energy crisis was sure to feature on his agenda.
